structure.overview: The case concerns a judicial review of the Refugee Appeal Division's (RAD) decision to exclude the Applicant from refugee protection under Article 1(E) due to alleged fraudulent evidence and residence issues in Spain. The Applicant challenges the RAD's decision as unreasonable and procedurally unfair, while the Respondent defends the RAD's authority and findings. The Federal Court finds the RAD's decision reasonable and procedurally fair, dismissing the Applicant's judicial review application.

party_points.text: decision unreasonable and breaches procedural fairness
RAD had authority to hear appeals and substitute RPD decision
RAD reasonably concluded residence permit needed for EU travel; no error ignoring investigation consent

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicant argues the decision is unreasonable and breaches procedural fairness.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court finds the RAD's decision reasonable and procedurally fair, dismissing the judicial review application.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The RPD found the Applicant was not excluded under Article 1(E) and accepted his refugee claim, noting only fraudulent TRV evidence of residence in Spain.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The RAD allowed the appeal against the RPD decision on December 19, 2022.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The RAD found the Applicant breached procedural fairness by not providing post-hearing evidence of an additional passport to the Respondent.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The RAD acknowledged evidence of the Applicant's residence in Spain but noted unexplained travel and work in the Schengen area without valid visas.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The RAD found the Applicant's second passport lacked work permits but showed EU travel stamps, concluding he held permanent residence in Spain.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Respondent established a prima facie exclusion case under Article 1(E), which the Applicant failed to rebut, leading to exclusion from protection.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Both parties agree on reasonableness for merits review; the court agrees and applies correctness for procedural fairness issues.

citations.cite: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65
citations.why: Sets reasonableness standard for merits review
Sets correctness standard for procedural fairness

citations.cite: Canadian Pacific Railway Company v Canada (Attorney General), 2018 FCA 69
citations.why: Supports correctness standard for procedural fairness

citations.cite: Canadian Association of Refugee Lawyers v Canada (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship), 2020 FCA 196
citations.why: Supports correctness standard for procedural fairness

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Reasonableness is deferential but robust, requiring transparent, justified, and coherent decisions based on facts and law.

citations.why: Defines reasonableness standard and its application

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: To find unreasonableness, flaws must be central; courts must not reweigh evidence or interfere absent exceptional circumstances.

citations.why: Limits on interference and defining significant flaws for unreasonableness

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Correctness is non-deferential; procedural fairness is assessed by fairness of procedure considering Baker factors.

citations.cite: Baker v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1999] 2 SCR 817 at paras 21-28
citations.why: Sets factors for assessing procedural fairness

citations.cite: Canadian Pacific Railway Company at para 54

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Respondent argues the RAD had authority to hear appeals and substitute the RPD decision.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court agrees with the Respondent that exclusion was not a new issue and the RAD had authority to substitute the RPD decision without oral evidence.

citations.cite: Kwakwa v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 600 at para 25
Kreishan v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FCA 223 at para 44
citations.why: Confirms RAD's power to set aside and substitute decisions

citations.cite: Huruglica v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FCA 93 at para 103
citations.why: Explains when RAD may refer matter back to RPD

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Respondent submits the RAD reasonably concluded the Applicant needed a residence permit for EU travel and did not err ignoring investigation consent.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court agrees the RAD independently assessed the record, substituted the RPD decision, and found no unreasonableness.

citations.why: Supports RAD's substitution of RPD decision

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The RAD did not err by not mentioning the Applicant's authorization to investigate; presumption is it considered all evidence.

citations.cite: Wang v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 546 at para 23
citations.why: Presumption that tribunal considers all evidence

citations.cite: Ruszo v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 943 at para 34
citations.why: Supports presumption of consideration of evidence

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The judicial review application is dismissed; the RAD's decision is reasonable and procedurally fair; no certification questions arise.
